question: A solenoid behaves like a magnet because:

options.text: Current in its turns produces a magnetic field

solution:
The correct answer is __**Current in its turns produces a magnetic field**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

 
• A solenoid is a long coil of wire wound in the shape of a cylinder. When an electric current flows through its turns, it produces a **magnetic field**.
 
• The magnetic field inside a solenoid is nearly uniform and strong, resembling the magnetic field of a bar magnet. This property makes it behave like a magnet.
 
• The strength of the magnetic field produced depends on factors such as the number of turns in the solenoid, the current passing through it, and the material of the core (if any).
 
• When the solenoid is wound around a magnetic material like iron, its magnetic field becomes even stronger due to the material's high magnetic permeability.
 
• This principle of solenoids is widely used in electromagnets, which are employed in various applications like electric bells, relays
